title: Chapter Fifty: Bibi
bio: “Bibi” — in the Classic of Mountains and Seas, the Eastern Mountains, there is Mount Gufeng. A beast lives there, shaped like a fox but with wings, its voice like a wild goose, and its name is Bibi; where it appears, the whole land falls into drought. As the saying goes: a fox’s face with wings, a cry like a wild goose — when the wind rises from the tip of the duckweed, what waits on the parched earth is a rain of blood in which nothing green survives.
paragraphs: Wu You was seldom back in town. Before heading to Shanghai he had asked Zheng Zhiyong to come and talk in his own office at the company. Old Zheng pulled the heavy wooden door shut behind him. The pressure in the room seemed to drop by half. The two men sat at opposite ends of the long sofa, the distance between them neither far nor near, but steeped in a subtle, testing reserve.

Wu You leaned back against the sofa, his tone unhurried, yet carrying a certainty that put a man at ease: “Mr. Zheng, the books are still only breaking even — no real profit squeezed out yet — but the annual frame contract for the night-vision equipment programme is signed and sealed. A solid five-year order; even as one of three suppliers we hold more than twenty percent. And the outside-processing quotes were driven down another notch in the end. You and the technical team did a fine job on cost control.”

It was one of the rare occasions when Wu You was unstinting in his praise of Old Zheng, and his eyes held both appraisal and approval: “Mr. Zheng, these two years you have done well by your people. That a group of technical men like Zhang Hailu and his lot could be brought in by you — and stay on at Xinghuan with their hearts in it — is to your credit. The business has steadied; next year we can count on a profit in the millions at the very least. And if the Xi’an tender makes a splash, then the year after, Xinghuan is a company with tens of millions in profit. Old Zheng, how far you have come these few years — everyone can see it.”
Then the subject turned, just slightly, and the temperature in the air seemed to fall a few degrees.

“I have sounded out the mood among the shareholders too. They are unanimous in agreeing to put the ten percent management equity we promised into the business registration properly. And though there is no dividend on the books this year, the board has decided that at year-end you get a bonus of five hundred thousand.”

Wu You looked at Old Zheng, his eyes as calm as still water. This was a late-night talk in which sugar coating and grave promises were woven together — an affirmation, and at the same time the deepest kind of tethering.
Yet at these words, Old Zheng was strangely calm.

Only a year ago, at about this time, he had been running himself ragged over the equity question, flying to Shanghai with Shasha to fight for it. Now, hearing this long-delayed promise finally honoured, he felt not a ripple. The reason was simple — he had long since stopped treating Xinghuan’s charity as his only way out. At this moment he had, in the world outside, a road of retreat and a ground to stand on that were his own.

Old Zheng straightened a little, and said with a smile, neither servile nor overbearing: “Mr. Wu, I have never been in a hurry about the shares. If you say it will be handled this week, then I am truly grateful to you and the shareholders for the recognition. I will certainly keep at it and do the project in hand well.”

“Only,” Old Zheng paused, “I can understand having the staff sign non-compete agreements. But the finance people bringing a non-compete agreement to me to sign — is that the two Mr. Wu’s way of saying you do not trust me?”
Wu You said, startled: “Mr. Zheng, I think you may be overthinking this. Wu Peng told me about it — it is a confidentiality requirement from the project side. That is common practice, surely.”

Zheng Zhiyong answered: “I am afraid it is not so common. I think that since I hold shares in Xinghuan, I am an owner too, and Mr. Wu ought to have confidence in my commitment to this platform.” Wu You thought for a moment, and decided not to insist on the agreement any further. He clapped Old Zheng on the shoulder. The two exchanged a few more pleasantries and went their separate ways.

One by one the lights in the building went out; only in Old Zheng’s office a single lamp still burned. He sat at his desk, having just that evening come away with equity and a five-hundred-thousand bonus, and yet he knew better than anyone: capital’s honey always comes with a shackle. The more Wu You used interest to soothe him and tie him down at this particular moment, the more it proved how vital tomorrow’s decisive tender battle was to Xinghuan. And by holding the non-compete signing in abeyance, Wu You had left a door open for Old Zheng’s own future possibilities. In fact, if Wu You had insisted today, Old Zheng knew he would have had no grounds to keep refusing. But why had he not insisted?

And it was precisely because he had not insisted that Old Zheng understood: at this moment he should still hold his ground on Xinghuan’s position, and with Wu You and Zhang Hailu take on Diao Kexin and her people in this contest. Right now the card he kept in the encrypted hard drive of his computer was waiting quietly for the horn to sound and the table to open.
In the conference room of Xinghuan Technology in the Xi’an High-Tech Zone science park, every light was on, and the air was thick with strong coffee and the rise and fall of tobacco smoke.

Only a few hours remained before the deadline for submitting materials for the Sixth Academy project. The whiteboard was crammed with technical parameters, simulation models and the talking points for the defence. Zhang Hailu and the technical team had gone two whole nights without sleep; his eyes were red-rimmed and his beard unkempt, but his gaze held a feverish, almost crazed excitement. Dr. Lan sat at a computer in the corner, fingers flying over the keyboard as he ran a stress test on the final version of the underlying algorithm, while Zhang Hailu went through all thousand-odd pages of documents for one last check and confirmation.
Old Zheng pushed the door open, carrying several large boxes of pizza, chicken wings, snacks and hot coffee.

“Hailu, Dr. Lan, thank you all for your hard work.” Old Zheng set the pizza down on the table and clapped Zhang Hailu on the shoulder. “Get through this tonight, hand in the work, and then everyone go home and rest.” The team members came over to help themselves.
Zhang Hailu took a slice of pizza and stuffed it into his mouth: “Old Zheng, we are more or less done. Rest easy — one last check from me and I can submit the whole bid package into the system.”

“You have all been pushing yourselves hard lately. Take tomorrow morning off — everyone come in late.” Old Zheng said this to them all, and the tension in the room instantly eased; the younger colleagues even clapped.
Yet Old Zheng did not know that at this moment there was another matter weighing on Zhang Hailu’s mind. A few hours earlier, a message had flashed up on his phone.
It had come that evening, from Diao Kexin: “Brother Hailu, I am at the Shangri-La in Xi’an. If you have time, shall the two of us catch up?”

Given what had happened before, at their private meeting in Xiangtan, Zhang Hailu naturally knew what Diao Kexin meant by it. A few hours later, after he had sent Xinghuan’s final proposal into the project owner’s online system just before the deadline and the work of the whole technical department could at last be set down, Zhang Hailu slipped quietly out of the office and, with a complicated heart, made his way to the Shangri-La Hotel Xi’an.

The revolving door of the hotel lobby turned slowly, and warm air rushed in. Zhang Hailu had not sat long on a sofa in the lobby before he saw the familiar figure come from the direction of the lifts — Diao Kexin stepping out of the private elevator from the guest floors above.

She wore a grey knitted A-line dress that clung to the body, a metallic sheen of fine thread woven into the texture of the fabric, the hem falling exactly at the knee. Her long hair was tied back neatly, her face carried an impeccable, exquisite makeup, and she was every inch the mature woman’s allure — and at this moment she was still wearing a pair of the hotel’s towelling slippers, standing there before Zhang Hailu with a willowy grace.
“Brother Hailu — oh, the lobby seems a bit cold. Would you like to come upstairs with me and sit?” Diao Kexin came up to him on a faint drift of scent and said it lightly, softly.
Zhang Hailu raised his eyelids and looked at her, and spoke calmly: “Ms. Diao, it is a little late now. I will not go up — it would not be appropriate.”

At that, Diao Kexin was not in the least offended; instead she leaned in slightly, the corner of her mouth curving into a smile full of meaning. She looked at Zhang Hailu and let her voice soften a little more:

“Brother Hailu, do not let your thoughts run astray. I was thinking — this is Xi’an, your company’s own territory. If the two of us meet privately and some acquaintance sees us, that would not be good. My room is a suite; in a moment we can sit on the sofa in the outer room and have some tea. How about that?”

So Zhang Hailu obediently went upstairs with Diao Kexin. She went back into the room, and it was as she had said: the two of them sat on the sofa in the outer room, she poured him a glass of hot water, then made tea with a tea bag, and settled naturally into the single armchair opposite him. She pulled the band from her ponytail in one motion and ran a hand through it, and the strands fell loose and compliant over her shoulders. Then she said: “Brother Hailu, last time you said you would go back and think it over. How have you thought it through?”

Faced with an assault so bare-faced, Zhang Hailu’s heart did give a small lurch. He knew only too well what Diao Kexin was about at this moment, and the terms she had offered last time were not ungenerous — above all the chance to go home and look after his wife and daughter. His heart had been wavering since that day. But what held him back now was not only his own coming or going, but the whole team he had brought with him.

Zhang Hailu drew a deep breath and leaned back, his tone cooling: “Ms. Diao, your terms last time were indeed very tempting. But my practical difficulty now is that I have already put down roots here with an entire team. If I leave by myself, I cannot take these brothers with me. You know what Old Zheng is like — his technical skill is real, and after two years of fighting side by side with him there is real feeling there. I am afraid I may have to let your kindness pass.”

The smile on Diao Kexin’s face did not change in the slightest, and her eyes stayed gentle. She looked at Zhang Hailu tenderly and said: “Brother Hailu, if I am not mistaken, the team you mean is also the brothers who came over from Yuanwang back then. Count it for me — if you were to take the most important members of your team with you, how many would there be, and what would their monthly cost come to?”

Zhang Hailu actually did reckon it up, one by one, honestly: the most important were Dr. Lan and a few other technical mainstays; not counting those hired and trained locally later, about four people, at a total monthly cost of around a hundred and twenty or thirty thousand. Diao Kexin said: “Bring the whole team — so much the better. Besides the salary I promised you last time, which will be honoured, everyone who comes over gets a fixed salary fifty percent above what Xinghuan pays now, with bonuses on top.”

The figure very nearly knocked Zhang Hailu senseless, but he steadied himself and said: “Ms. Diao, I hear the company is carrying debt and that finance is tight. How can you be sure you can keep a crowd like us fed?”

Diao Kexin went into the inner room, and after a moment came out with a technical document. She let Zhang Hailu look at it briefly, and said: “This is our algorithm architecture. It should be a good long way better than the proposal you have now.”

One glance was enough to make Zhang Hailu draw a sharp breath. After all, he had been fighting this matter for weeks; seeing the architecture, he knew at once that this scheme was far superior to Xinghuan’s. So the strategy of Zhu Yiwen and Diao Kexin had been to take the best combination, the optimal architecture, the lowest cost and the upper-level relationships, and deliver them all through Yuanwang. Zhu Yiwen’s Gaoda was not there to bid in a ring around the tender — it was there to accompany the bid.

There were now only some ten minutes left before midnight. The deadline for the several parties to submit their schemes to the online system was almost upon them. Zhang Hailu understood that the timber was already a boat; and in his heart he knew that this time Diao Kexin and her side had far too much of the winning hand.
Zhang Hailu said: “If your scheme is that good, why do you still need our team?”

Diao Kexin said: “If we win this project, and the core technology of the technical scheme is not in my own company’s hands — that is, if an outside supplier holds the pricing power over the whole thing — then I am entirely at a disadvantage. As it is, I have this technology’s architecture and principles complete and in my hands. If you come over and study it thoroughly, you should be able to take it on and build it out. Am I right?”
Zhang Hailu nodded.
At that same hour, at two in the morning, Old Zheng returned to his own quarters on the fourth floor.
The whole building had sunk into a dead silence. Old Zheng had come back to the flat that was his to use, at the top of the building above the offices.

The computer screen cast back the reflection of his bloodshot eyes. He was not looking at the defence slides he still had to prepare; he had opened an encrypted file. The material inside it was enough to drag that woman — who had already walked out of the storm once — back down into the abyss.

The decisive battle between Old Zheng and her was already coiled and waiting. When tomorrow’s sun rose, this business war and tangle of feeling, months long, would at last come to its bloodiest reckoning.
